newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac's office denies imminent reshuffle, poll.
newsitem.headline: Chirac's office denies imminent reshuffle, poll.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac's office on Wednesday poured cold water on rumours that he planned to shortly reshuffle the centre-right cabinet or bring forward a parliamentary election scheduled in March next year.
After a day of increasing speculation in political circles, an official source at Chirac's Elysee presidential palace said the rumours were "without foundation".
The source said: "All of this is absolutely not on the agenda."
But the source left open the possibility that Chirac may take some sort of political initiative in the near future by adding: "The president has time on his hands for reflection."
Education Minister Francois Bayrou, a leader of the centrist Union for French Democracy (UDF), the Gaullists' junior partner in the ruling coalition, indicated a move may be on the cards.
"The president and the prime minister are reflecting. Let them carry out this reflection," he told reporters.

Politicians and analysts speculated that Chirac might take advantage of disarray in the Socialist opposition to call an early election, hoping to renew the favourable centre-right majority for the remainder of his seven-year term.
An early poll would also help avoid a collision between the election timetable and European Union plans to select countries early in 1998 to take part in a single European currency from 1999.
Analysts believed that, alternatively, a reshuffle would enable Juppe's cabinet to streamline itself ahead of the election campaign.

A reshuffle might allow reconciliation with some leading centre-right politicians whose ties with Chirac soured when they backed his fellow-Gaullist rival, ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur, in the 1995 presidential elections.
The rumours increased after Juppe held unscheduled talks on Wednesday with former defence minister Francois Leotard, the head of the UDF and a former Balladur backer.
Juppe had earlier declined to discuss the rumours, merely telling reporters after an unusually brief weekly cabinet meeting: "Oh no, I cannot comment."
